questions.title: Light microscopic picture of platelets
questions.question: What is the light microscopic picture of platelets?

options.C: Irregular cell membrane with thick cell coat
options.E: Their outer part is dark stained (granulomere)

explanations.A: Incorrect. Biconcavity is the erythrocyte's shape, not the platelet's. Platelets are oval-to-round fragments, not biconcave discs, and confusing the two shapes is a common mistake because both are anucleate.
explanations.B: Correct. On light microscopy a platelet is a small, oval, non-nucleated disc, roughly 2-4 micrometres across. It is a cytoplasmic fragment budded from a megakaryocyte, so it never had a nucleus to lose, unlike the erythrocyte which extrudes one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The platelet's plasma membrane is a regular lipid bilayer with a surface coat, not a distinctively thick or irregular one; irregularity of outline is not how platelets are identified under the light microscope.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The hyalomere (the pale peripheral zone) and granulomere (the dark central zone) are an electron-microscopic and special-stain distinction inside a single platelet, not what defines its light-microscopic outline; describing only the inner zone leaves out the platelet's overall appearance.
explanations.E: Incorrect. As with the hyalomere, the granulomere is one internal zone of the platelet, not a description of the whole cell's light-microscopic picture, which the oval non-nucleated disc already covers.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the platelet's light-microscopic appearance as a small, oval, non-nucleated disc.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.16

questions.title: Largest cell in thrombopoiesis
questions.question: The largest cell in thrombopoiesis is:

explanations.A: Correct. The megakaryocyte, the mature stage of thrombopoiesis, is the largest cell in the bone marrow, up to 100 micrometres across. It reaches that size because it becomes polyploid through repeated endomitosis without cell division, which multiplies its DNA content and cytoplasmic volume many times over. Only after that growth does it fragment its cytoplasm into individual platelets.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The pro-megakaryocyte precedes the megakaryocyte in the series and is smaller; size increases as the series progresses toward the fully polyploid megakaryocyte, not before it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The megakaryoblast is the earliest recognisable precursor in the series and is smaller than the cells that follow it, well before the endomitotic enlargement that makes the megakaryocyte the largest.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The promyelocyte belongs to the granulocyte series (granulopoiesis), not thrombopoiesis, and answering it here confuses the two myeloid lineages.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The proerythroblast belongs to the erythroid series (erythropoiesis), not thrombopoiesis, and it is a small early precursor, not a large cell.

questions.learning_objective: Name the megakaryocyte as the largest cell in thrombopoiesis and explain why endomitosis makes it so large.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.16

questions.title: Normal platelet life span
questions.question: What is the normal life span of platelets?

explanations.A: Incorrect. 1-2 days is far shorter than a platelet's real circulating life span; a lifespan this short would make normal haemostasis impossible to sustain between marrow replenishment cycles.
explanations.B: Correct. Platelets circulate for about 7-10 days before being removed, mainly by the spleen. This is far shorter than the erythrocyte's roughly 120-day lifespan, reflecting the platelet's role as a short-lived, rapidly replenished haemostatic fragment rather than a long-lived circulating cell.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 30-35 days overstates the platelet's lifespan by roughly a factor of four; no blood cell type in this bank has that specific value as its correct lifespan.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 1-2 months is closer to some white cell tissue lifespans than to the platelet's short circulating life; platelets do not persist in circulation this long.
explanations.E: Incorrect. 5-10 months is an order of magnitude too long for any circulating blood cell in this series, platelet included.

questions.learning_objective: State the platelet's normal circulating life span (7-10 days) and contrast it with the erythrocyte's longer lifespan.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.16

questions.title: Normal platelet count
questions.question: Normal platelet count:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 10,000-15,000/mm3 is roughly an order of magnitude below the true normal platelet range; a count this low would already be a significant thrombocytopenia.
explanations.B: Correct. The normal platelet count is about 150,000-400,000/mm3 (commonly cited as roughly 300,000/mm3 as a working average). This range is what separates a normal count from thrombocytopenia below it and thrombocytosis above it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 4,000-11,000/mm3 is the normal range for total white blood cells, not platelets; the two counts are easy to confuse because both are reported per cubic millimetre.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 4-5.5 million/mm3 is in the range of the red blood cell count, not the platelet count; platelets are far less numerous than erythrocytes.
explanations.E: Incorrect. 4.5-6 million/mm3 is likewise an erythrocyte-range value, not a platelet count.

questions.learning_objective: State the normal platelet count (150,000-400,000/mm3) and distinguish it from the white cell and red cell reference ranges.

questions.title: Contents of platelet delta (dense) granules
questions.question: Delta granules of platelets contain:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Lysosomes are their own separate organelle inside the platelet, not a content of the delta (dense) granule; they carry the platelet's own hydrolytic enzymes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Platelet-derived growth factor is stored in the alpha granule, not the delta (dense) granule — the two granule types are a common paired distractor in this bank and carry different contents.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mitochondria are separate organelles that supply the platelet's energy; they are not packaged inside a delta granule.
explanations.D: Correct. The delta (dense) granule stores serotonin, along with ADP and calcium. It releases them on platelet activation, once the platelet has bound to exposed collagen at a site of vessel injury. That release recruits and aggregates further circulating platelets to build the platelet plug.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Platelets are anucleate cytoplasmic fragments and contain no DNA at all, whether inside a granule or otherwise.

questions.learning_objective: Name serotonin, ADP and calcium as the delta (dense) granule's contents, as distinct from the alpha granule's growth-factor cargo.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.17

questions.title: Platelet development and the megakaryocyte nucleus
questions.question: Regarding platelet development:

options.D: Megakaryocyte has a large lobulated nucleus
options.E: Pro-megakaryocytes are small with acidophilic non-granular cytoplasm

explanations.A: Incorrect. Thrombopoiesis is stimulated mainly by thrombopoietin, not erythropoietin; erythropoietin drives the separate erythroid (red cell) series.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The megakaryoblast, the earliest cell in the series, has basophilic (not acidophilic) and agranular (not granular) cytoplasm; granularity develops later, in the megakaryocyte itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The megakaryocyte is the largest cell in the marrow, not a small one — the opposite of what this option states, and a direct contradiction of its own defining feature.
explanations.D: Correct. The megakaryocyte's large, lobulated (multilobed) nucleus is one of its two defining features, alongside its very large polyploid cell size. Both arise from repeated endomitosis — DNA replication without cell division — which multiplies the nuclear DNA content into one large lobulated nucleus rather than several separate ones.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Pro-megakaryocytes are larger than the megakaryoblast that precedes them, not small, and their cytoplasm is beginning to show granules as the series progresses toward the megakaryocyte, not remaining non-granular.

questions.learning_objective: State that the megakaryocyte's large size and lobulated nucleus both result from endomitosis, and that thrombopoiesis is thrombopoietin-driven, not erythropoietin-driven.

questions.title: Thrombocytes and blood clotting (past-exam block, دفعة 62)
questions.question: Which of the following blood cells play a role in blood clotting?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Erythrocytes carry oxygen and carbon dioxide; they are not the cell type responsible for the platelet plug and clot formation of haemostasis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Monocytes are phagocytic cells that become tissue macrophages; clotting is not their function.
explanations.C: Correct. Thrombocytes (platelets) are the blood cell responsible for clotting. They aggregate at a site of vessel injury and activate, exposing a phospholipid surface. That surface, together with the contents released from their granules, drives the coagulation cascade forward to a stable clot.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Neutrophils are the first line of non-specific phagocytic defence against bacteria; they play no direct role in the clotting mechanism.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Basophils release histamine and heparin in inflammatory and allergic responses; heparin is in fact an anticoagulant, the opposite of a clotting role.

questions.learning_objective: Identify thrombocytes (platelets) as the blood cell responsible for clotting, as distinct from the other named leukocytes.

questions.title: The smallest blood cell (past-exam block, دفعة 63)
questions.question: The smallest blood cell is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The erythrocyte, at about 7-7.5 micrometres, is larger than the platelet.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Even the small lymphocyte, the smallest nucleated leukocyte, is larger than an anucleate platelet fragment.
explanations.C: Correct. The platelet, at roughly 2-4 micrometres, is the smallest formed element of the blood, smaller than any leukocyte and smaller than the erythrocyte. It is this small because it is only a cytoplasmic fragment budded from a megakaryocyte, not a whole cell. That fragment nature, not a shrunken whole cell, is why it has no nucleus and no room for the organelles a full cell would carry.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The monocyte is the largest leukocyte in a normal blood smear, the opposite extreme from the smallest blood cell asked for here.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The neutrophil, at 10-12 micrometres, is far larger than the platelet.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the platelet as the smallest formed element of the blood.
